interactive.title: The hinge
interactive.whatAmILookingAt: A short lesson in fifteen small screens. Most use one picture, the hinge: two straight arms joined at a corner, arm a 3 long and arm b 4 long, in any unit, with the angle C between them, which you open and close by dragging the free end of arm a. The third side, c, is drawn between the two free ends, with its length read out. Each side is named with the small letter of the corner opposite it. Under the hinge stand three bars on one scale. The first is a² + b², 25, and it stays put because the arms do not change. The second is the correction, −2ab cos C, which is 24 × cos C taken away: it hangs below the zero line, dashed, while C is under 90°, is empty at 90°, and stands above the line past 90°, because there the cosine is negative and taking away a negative adds. The third is c², the first bar plus the correction, and it matches the square of the drawn side at every angle. A readout gives cos C to three decimal places with its sign. At 90° a small square marks the right angle and a label says Pythagoras. Screen 1 shows the hinge at 90°, where c is 5, then sweeps it between 60° and 120° and back to 90°, so you see c fall below Pythagoras' 5 and rise above it. Screen 2 asks which is c at 120°: 6.08, 5 or 3.61. Screen 3 builds the rule: arm b lies along the across axis from the corner, arm a is lesson 3's turning arm scaled up to length a, its tip at (a cos C, a sin C), and dashed lines mark the gap to the end of arm b, labelled b − a cos C across and a sin C up; the working then appears one line at a time below the picture, ending at c² = a² + b² − 2ab cos C. Screen 4 asks for c² at 60°: 13, 19 (the 2 dropped) or 0.5 (25 − 24 worked first, then multiplied by 0.5). Screen 5 opens the hinge to 110° and on to 180°, where the arms lie flat and c = 7, then closes it to 0°, where they fold together and c = 1. Screen 6 asks for c at 110°: 5.76, 4.10 (the cosine's minus sign lost) or 1.56 (sin 110° used). Screen 7 runs the rule backwards with three sides, 3, 4 and 6: cos C = (9 + 16 − 36) ÷ 24 = −0.458, so C = 117.3°, and the hinge swings to that angle as the working appears. Screen 8 asks for the angle opposite the side of 7 in a triangle with sides 5, 7 and 8: 60°, 120° (the subtraction the wrong way round) or 38.2° (the angle opposite the side of 5). Screen 9 drops a height from corner B square onto side AC and finds it twice, as c sin A and as a sin C, which gives the sine rule; if A is past 90° the height lands outside, beyond A, and sin (180° − A) = sin A keeps the rule the same. Screen 10 asks for side b when A = 40°, B = 60° and a = 5: 6.74, 3.71 (the sines upside down) or 7.5 (the angles divided instead of their sines). Screens 11 and 12 use a second picture, the swing arm: a base line from corner A, a side b of 8 at a fixed angle A of 30° up to corner C, and from C an arm a whose length you set with a slider. It swings round C, and every point where its end meets the base line becomes a corner B, with its triangle drawn and its angle B labelled. On screen 11 the height from C to the base line is 4, so an arm of 3 falls short; at 5 it lands twice, B = 53.1° or 126.9°; at 8 the second landing reaches A itself, and longer it falls behind A, so either way one triangle is left. Screen 12 sets a = 6 and asks which angles B fit: 41.8° and 138.2°, 41.8° only, or 41.8° and 318.2°. Screens 13 to 15 are mixed, so you choose the rule from what you are given. Two ships sail from one port, 48 and 40 nautical miles, on courses 113° apart: are they 73.5, 62.5 (Pythagoras) or 49.0 (the cosine's sign lost) nautical miles apart? Then a triangle with a right angle between sides of 5 and 2: which finds the angle θ opposite the 2 in one step, tan θ = 2 ÷ 5, giving 21.8°, the cosine rule (it would need the third side first) or the sine rule (no known side faces a known angle)? Last, a puzzle labelled on screen as a stretch, on an engine with example figures: the crankshaft centre, the crankpin and the piston pin make a triangle, with a crank of 50 mm, a connecting rod of 200 mm and the crank turned 40° from the cylinder's centre line. Is the rod's angle to the centre line 9.2° only, 9.2° or 170.8°, or no such triangle, the slip of putting each side over the wrong angle, where the sine comes out at 2.571, and no sine is over 1, so sin⁻¹ shows an error? Each puzzle offers three answers; a wrong pick gets a one-line hint naming its slip, and Why? draws the answer on the picture.
interactive.ignores: The arms are drawn as lines meeting at a single point, so a real hinge's thickness and pivot are left out. Lengths are example figures, in no particular unit unless a screen names one. Readouts are rounded, cosines and sines to three decimal places, sides to two and angles to one, while the working keeps every figure. At 0° and 180° the hinge has gone flat and there is no triangle, but the rule still gives the gap between the free ends, the arms' difference or their sum.

explain.text:
Sine, cosine and tangent, as lesson 1 built them, need a right angle. Plenty of real triangles have none: two ships on different courses, an engine's crank and its connecting rod. Two rules solve them. The cosine rule is Pythagoras with a correction for the angle, and the sine rule says that each side divided by the sine of the angle opposite it gives the same number all round the triangle.

Picture two straight arms joined at a hinge, a long and b long, with the angle C between them. Name each side with the small letter of the corner opposite it, so the third side, joining the arms' free ends, is c. At 90° Pythagoras gives c² = a² + b². Close the hinge and the free ends come together, so c is shorter than at 90°; open it and they move apart, so c is longer. To find by how much, lay arm b along the across axis from the hinge, so its free end is at (b, 0). Arm a is then lesson 3's turning arm. That arm was 1 long with its tip at (cos C, sin C),[^1] and an arm a long is the same shape scaled up, so its tip is at (a cos C, a sin C). The gap between the free ends is b − a cos C across and a sin C up, and Pythagoras on that gap gives c² = (b − a cos C)² + (a sin C)². Multiplied out, that is b² − 2ab cos C + a² cos² C + a² sin² C. Lesson 3's cos² C + sin² C = 1 turns the last two terms into a², which leaves c² = a² + b² − 2ab cos C. This is the [[cosine rule]]: the square of a side is the sum of the squares of the other two, minus twice their product and the cosine of the angle between them.[^2] It is Pythagoras with something extra, so it works for all triangles.[^3]

The correction, −2ab cos C, is where the angle comes in. At 90° the cosine is 0, so the correction vanishes and the rule is Pythagoras. Below 90° the cosine is positive, so the correction takes away. Past 90° the arm's tip has swung left of the hinge, so the cosine is negative,[^4] taking away a negative adds, and c comes out longer than Pythagoras gives. With arms 3 and 4, a² + b² = 25 and 2ab = 24. At 60°, cos 60° = 0.5, so c² = 25 − 24 × 0.5 = 13 and c = 3.61. At 110°, cos 110° = −0.342, so c² = 25 + 8.21 = 33.21 and c = 5.76. The rule finds a side from two sides and the angle between them, or an angle from all three sides.[^5] For the angle, rearrange it to cos C = (a² + b² − c²) ÷ 2ab, with c the side opposite the angle you want, and press cos⁻¹. Each angle from 0° to 180° has a cosine of its own, so cos⁻¹ gives the one angle that fits, acute or obtuse.

The sine rule comes from dropping a height. In a triangle ABC, drop a line from B square onto side AC, carried on past A or C if the triangle leans over. It makes two right-angled triangles, and lesson 1's sine gives the height twice: c sin A from one and a sin C from the other. So c sin A = a sin C, and dividing both sides by sin A sin C gives a ÷ sin A = c ÷ sin C. If A is past 90° the height lands outside the triangle, beyond A, where the angle beside it is 180° − A, and lesson 3 showed sin (180° − A) = sin A, so nothing changes; the same goes for C. A height from another corner brings in b the same way, so a ÷ sin A = b ÷ sin B = c ÷ sin C. This is the [[sine rule]]: each side over the sine of the angle opposite it.[^6] Use it for a side from another side and two angles, or for an angle from two sides and an angle that is not between them.[^7] For an angle there is a catch. Lesson 3 showed that θ and 180° − θ share a sine, so sin⁻¹ gives one angle, and 180° minus it may fit as well. It fits only if the triangle's angles still come to less than 180°, leaving room for the third.[^8] When the same facts fit two triangles, it is called the [[ambiguous case]]. **The cosine rule, c² = a² + b² − 2ab cos C,[^2] is Pythagoras with a correction that takes away below 90° and adds past it; the sine rule pairs each side with the sine of the angle opposite it, and when it finds an angle, 180° minus that angle may fit too.[^8]**

analogy.text: Open two leaves of a folding rule to a right angle and the gap between their tips is Pythagoras on the two leaves. Close them and the gap shrinks below that; open them wider and it grows past it, until, laid flat, the gap is the two leaves end to end. The cosine rule gives the gap at every opening, with the correction as the amount the gap's square falls short of Pythagoras or runs over it.
analogy.breaks: A folding rule's leaves have thickness and their pivot sits a little in from the ends, so the tips' gap only comes near the rule's value, which is for straight lines meeting at a point. And the rule's leaves show nothing of the sine rule or its two possible triangles.

practice.text:
- Decide which rule from what you know. Two sides and the angle between them, or all three sides: the cosine rule.[^5] Two angles and a side, or two sides and an angle not between them: the sine rule.[^7] A right angle in the triangle: lesson 1's sine, cosine and tangent, or Pythagoras, are all you need.
- Label the corners A, B and C, and each side with the small letter of the corner opposite it.
- Set the calculator to degrees mode.[^9]
- Cosine rule for a side: work out a² + b², then 2ab cos C with the cosine's sign, take the second from the first, then take the square root.
- Cosine rule for an angle: cos C = (a² + b² − c²) ÷ 2ab, where c is the side opposite the angle you want, then cos⁻¹.
- Sine rule for an angle: sin⁻¹ gives one angle. Check 180° minus it too, which fits only if the angles still leave room under 180°.[^8]
- Keep each unrounded answer in the calculator for the next step, and round at the end.
- Check: the longest side faces the largest angle.

**Rule of thumb:** At 90° the cosine rule is Pythagoras. Wider than 90°, the third side is longer than Pythagoras gives; narrower, shorter.

**Worked example:** Say two sides of 7 m and 10 m meet at 50°. c² = 49 + 100 − 2 × 7 × 10 × cos 50° = 149 − 140 × cos 50° = 149 − 89.99 = 59.01, so c = 7.68 m. Now the angle A opposite the 7 m side, by the sine rule, with c kept unrounded: sin A = 7 × sin 50° ÷ 7.68 = 0.698, so A = 44.3°. Its partner, 180° − 44.3° = 135.7°, would make 135.7° + 50° = 185.7°, past 180°, so it does not fit. The third angle is 180° − 50° − 44.3° = 85.7°.

**Common mistakes**
- Using sine, cosine, tangent or Pythagoras on a triangle with no right angle. Pythagoras on arms of 3 and 4 gives 5 at any opening; at 60° the third side is 3.61.
- Dropping the 2: 25 − 12 × 0.5 = 19, not 13.
- Taking away before multiplying: (25 − 24) × 0.5 = 0.5. Multiply 2ab by the cosine first, then take it away.
- Losing the cosine's minus sign past 90°. cos 110° is −0.342, so the correction adds.
- Using sin C where the rule has cos C.
- An error from cos⁻¹ means the number was above 1 or below −1, which no cosine can be. Check that 2ab is made from the two sides you squared and added, and that the longest side is shorter than the other two together, or there is no triangle.
- Stopping at the sine rule's first angle when 180° minus it fits too.

interactive.html: A hinge of two arms for the cosine rule, a dropped height and a swinging arm for the sine rule, then three mixed puzzles.
interactive.title: The hinge
interactive.brief: The one thing you should see is the correction bar, −2ab cos C, taking away below 90°, empty at 90° and adding past it, when you open and close the hinge.

checks.label: The square of any side of a triangle is equal to the sum of the squares of the other two sides minus twice the product of the other two sides and the cosine of the included angle: at every whole angle of the hinge from 0° to 180°, the third side measured off the drawing, squared, is 9 + 16 − 24 cos C, the c² bar stands exactly that high on the bars' scale, it is the first bar and the correction together, and the side's label and the bar's label agree

It helps to know it's the Pythagoras Theorem with something extra so it works for all triangles: at 90° the hinge shows a right-angle square and the label Pythagoras, the correction is 0 and c = 5, and at every other whole angle from 0° to 180° the correction is not zero and neither the square nor the label is shown

Sine, cosine and tangent all have different positive or negative values depending on what quadrant they are in: at every whole angle, the cos C readout is negative exactly when the tip of arm a is left of the hinge, past 90°, and then the correction bar stands above the zero line, solid; below 90° the readout is positive and the bar hangs below the line, dashed, with its key

The terminal side of the angle intersects the circle at the point (x, y), which is equivalent to (cos t, sin t): on the screen that builds the rule, arm a is lesson 3's arm made 3 times longer, so at every angle it can be dragged to, its tip measured off the drawing is 3 cos C across and 3 sin C up from the hinge, and the dashed gap to the end of arm b is 4 − 3 cos C across and 3 sin C up

The cosine rule is a formula used to find a missing side or angle in a triangle when two sides and included angle, or all the lengths of all three sides, are known: from sides 3, 4 and 6 it gives cos C = −0.458 and C = 117.3°, and the hinge opened to that angle draws a third side of exactly 6; from two sides and the angle between them it gives the side, 3.61 at 60°

The sine rule can find a side from another side and two angles or an angle from two sides and a non-included angle: in the drawn triangle with A = 40°, B = 60° and a = 5, side b measured off the drawing is 5 × sin 60° ÷ sin 40° = 6.74, and on the swing arm, with b = 8, A = 30° and an arm a of 5, the angle drawn at the first landing is 53.1°

The second answer is found by subtracting the first answer from 180°; if the angles in the triangle do not exceed the angle sum of a triangle, 180°, the second answer can exist: at every arm length from 2 to 9 on the swing-arm screen, a second triangle is drawn exactly when 30° plus 180° minus the first angle B is under 180°, its angle B is 180° minus the first, both landings lie on the base line exactly the arm's length from C, and an arm shorter than the height, 4, lands nowhere
Where a right angle makes lesson 1 enough: the drawn triangle measured off the drawing has sides 5 and 2 meeting square, and its angle opposite the 2 is tan⁻¹(2 ÷ 5) = 21.8°

A height dropped from B is found twice: on the height screen, the drawn height, measured off the drawing, equals c sin A and a sin C, with c, a and the angles A and C measured off the same drawing, so a ÷ sin A = c ÷ sin C there too

Every worked number matches the lesson: c = 5 at 90°; 6.08 and 37 at 120°; 3.61 and 13 at 60°, with slips 19 and 0.5; cos 110° = −0.342, a correction of 8.21, c² = 33.21 and c = 5.76, with slips 4.10 and 1.56; 7 laid flat and 1 folded; −0.458 and 117.3° from 3, 4 and 6; 60°, 120° and 38.2° from 5, 8 and 7; 6.74, 3.71 and 7.5; a height of 4, 0.8, 53.1° and 126.9°; 0.667, 41.8°, 138.2° and 318.2°; 73.5, 62.5 and 49.0 nautical miles, with 3840 and cos 113° = −0.390731; tan θ = 0.4 and 21.8° for the right angle; 0.161, 9.2° and 170.8°, and 2.571, over 1

Each puzzle accepts only its right answer, every wrong answer has its own hint and its own red row of working, the answer appears once it is given, and before an answer nothing in the picture gives it away

No label sits on another label or a handle, or runs off the picture, on any screen in any state: puzzles answered right, wrong or with Why? open, the hinge dragged to every angle, the arm set to every length
Every demonstration has finished within 4.5 s of its screen opening, none starting before the 0.35 s screen fade ends; each answer and Why? has settled within 1.8 s

applied.problem: Taking away a side other than the one opposite gives another angle of the triangle, never a cos⁻¹ error; the error comes from a 2ab that does not match the sides added, or from sides that cannot make a triangle (one as long as the other two together).
With b = 8 and A = 30°, an arm of exactly 8 has its second landing on A itself (C is 8 from A), not behind it; only longer arms land behind A. Either way one triangle is left.
